changes.before: **Same common divisors.** First with numbers. 3 divides 21, so it also divides 21 twice over: $$21 \times 2 = 42$$ 3 divides 51 too, so it divides the difference: $$51 - 42 = 9$$
changes.after: **Same common factors.** We want to show: a common factor of 51 and 21 is also a factor of the remainder 9. Take 3, a common factor of 51 and 21. Write both as multiples of 3: $$51 = 3 \times 17, \qquad 21 = 3 \times 7$$ The remainder is what's left of 51 after two 21s: $$9 = 51 - 2 \times 21$$ Replace 51 and 21 by their multiples of 3, and take the 3 out: $$\begin{aligned} 9 &= 3 \times 17 - 2 \times (3 \times 7) \\ &= 3 \times (17 - 14) \\ &= 3 \times 3 \end{aligned}$$ So 3 is a factor of 9.

changes.after: **In general.** We want to show: a common factor of $a$ and $b$ is also a factor of the remainder $r$. Take $h$, a common factor of $a$ and $b$. Write both as multiples of $h$: $$a = hx, \qquad b = hy$$ The remainder is what's left of $a$ after $q$ copies of $b$: $$r = a - qb$$ Replace $a$ and $b$ by their multiples of $h$, and take the $h$ out: $$\begin{aligned} r &= hx - q \times hy \\ &= h(x - qy) \end{aligned}$$ So $h$ is a factor of $r$. snapshot: **Real and virtual.** If the rays **really meet** at the image, the image is **real**. Light actually gets there, so it can be caught on a screen, like a projector's picture on a wall. snapshot: **Why.** From *Zeroes and coefficients*: $$(x - \alpha)(x - \beta) = x^2 - (\alpha + \beta)x + \alpha\beta$$ Call the third zero $\gamma$ (gamma), and multiply by one more factor, $(x - \gamma)$. Multiply the bracket first by $x$, then by $-\gamma$: $$\begin{aligned} &(x - \alpha)(x - \beta)(x - \gamma) \\ &= x\,\big(x^2 - (\alpha+\beta)x + \alpha\beta\big) - \gamma\,\big(x^2 - (\alpha+\beta)x + \alpha\beta\big) \\ &= x^3 - (\alpha+\beta)x^2 + \alpha\beta\,x - \gamma x^2 + (\alpha+\beta)\gamma\,x - \alpha\beta\gamma \end{aligned}$$ Now collect the $x^2$ terms and the $x$ terms: $(\alpha+\beta)\gamma = \beta\gamma + \gamma\alpha$, so $$\begin{aligned} &= x^3 - (\alpha + \beta + \gamma)x^2 \\ &\quad + (\alpha\beta + \beta\gamma + \gamma\alpha)x - \alpha\beta\gamma \end{aligned}$$

snapshot: To check whether one polynomial is a factor of another, divide. Remainder 0 means yes. Is $t^2 - 3$ a factor of $2t^4 + 3t^3 - 2t^2 - 9t - 12$? Divide, one step at a time: $$\begin{aligned} \tfrac{2t^4}{t^2} = 2t^2 &: \quad \text{left } 3t^3 + 4t^2 - 9t - 12 \\ \tfrac{3t^3}{t^2} = 3t &: \quad \text{left } 4t^2 - 12 \\ \tfrac{4t^2}{t^2} = 4 &: \quad \text{left } 0 \end{aligned}$$ So $$\begin{aligned} &2t^4 + 3t^3 - 2t^2 - 9t - 12 \\ &= (t^2 - 3)(2t^2 + 3t + 4) + 0 \end{aligned}$$ The remainder is 0, so yes.
